candidates.title: From Solo to Social Learning: Characterizing Recursive Social Improvement in LLMs
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can now improve themselves by revising the instructions they follow, and LLM agents are increasingly orchestrated to work together on complex problems. However, self-improvement methods typically optimize one system at a time, and multi-agent frameworks often have every model work toward a shared goal. We ask a different question. When each agent pursues its own reward, can self-improving LLMs learn from one another well enough to improve the whole population? We call this capability recursive social improvement. We study populations that revise skill files and choose whether, when, and whom to copy from. Independent search, learning from peers, and acting all share one token budget. In controlled environments, established social-learning algorithms benefit from peers, but three LLMs do not. They earn less reward per token than solo learners, and explore too narrowly or run out of tokens before acting. We then let the models write and revise their own skills. Observing peers changes how they improve, helping one model find useful skills sooner and another spend less on private search. Neither, however, outperforms independent learners at the same cost. Skills are copied, revised, and passed on, so one discovery can seed further search. Yet these exchanges concentrate the population around fewer independent discoveries. Together, these results show that LLMs can make learning more efficient by copying from peers, but not yet more effective.

candidates.title: The future of spatial energy planning: A shift toward social learning and participatory visioning
candidates.abstract: Participatory planning is increasingly used to address complex challenges such as deciding where and how the energy transition should be implemented. Yet it remains unclear what people learn through participatory planning processes and how this learning shapes collective outcomes. This study examines social learning in a participatory regional visioning process in Knonauer Amt, Switzerland. Using surveys conducted before and after the process, we compare changes in the perspectives of participants ( N = 46) with those of non-participating regional residents ( N = 703). Participants' perspectives on spatial planning and the energy transition became more closely aligned than those of the wider regional population, although substantial differences remained. Despite these differences, the process produced a shared regional vision. The findings show that people do not need to agree on everything to move forward together. Participatory visioning can create a shared direction even when differences remain.

candidates.title: Analysis code and supporting materials for "Neural arbitration between social learning strategies depends on others' reliability"
candidates.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
candidates.abstract: This deposit contains analysis code and supporting materials accompanying the manuscript “Neural arbitration between social learning strategies depends on others’ reliability.” The archive includes behavioral analyses, hierarchical computational models implemented in Stan, WAIC model comparison, parameter and model recovery, whole-brain and ROI-based fMRI analyses, and scripts for reproducing individual manuscript figure panels. Behavioral data, numerical summaries, fixed ROI masks, and figure outputs are included. Reproduction instructions are provided in README.md and PUBLICATION.html, with Python dependencies pinned in uv.lock. Individual neuroimaging derivatives and large model-fitting artifacts are not included. The code is released under the MIT License.

candidates.title: Social Learning Theory, Family Violence, Maladaptive Behaviors and Academic Achievement Among Secondary School Students in North-Central Nigeria: Implications for Guidance and Counselling
candidates.venue: JOURNAL OF HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL POLICY
candidates.abstract: Family violence can affect the behavioural and educational adjustment of secondary school students. This conceptual article examines the relevance of Social Learning Theory to the relationship among family violence, maladaptive behaviours, and academic achievement among secondary school students in North-Central Nigeria. Drawing on Bandura’s Social Learning Theory, the article explains how observation, modelling, imitation, reinforcement, and self regulation may influence students’ behavioural responses. Exposure to aggression, hostility, intimidation, and dysfunctional conflict resolution may encourage maladaptive behaviours that interfere with school adjustment, attendance, engagement, and academic achievement. However, these effects are not deterministic, as positive parental, teacher, peer, and counsellor modelling can promote adaptive behaviour and academic engagement. The article discusses implications for guidance and counselling, emphasising positive modelling, parental guidance, self-regulation, early identification, supportive counselling, and family–school collaboration. It concludes that theoretically informed and preventive guidance and counselling can help reduce negative behavioural learning and promote positive behavioural and academic outcomes among secondary school students in North-Central Nigeria.

candidates.title: Characterize the Neural Representation of Vicarious Threat and Safety Learning in Social Anxiety Disorder
candidates.abstract: This analysis plan describes a multivoxel fMRI investigation of neural representations underlying vicarious threat and safety learning during fear extinction in social anxiety disorder (SAD). The central research question is: can neural representations associated with vicarious threat and safety learning be detected during fear extinction phase in SAD, and how is it different from the neural representations of healthy controls (HC). The primary focus is on the updating process that occurs during extinction, when previously acquired threat and safety information is being revised in response to new experience by a demonstrator. Accordingly, the analyses are designed to characterize neural representations expressed while this updating process is occurring, rather than to classify participants or individual trials according to whether extinction learning is “successful” or “unsuccessful”. Learning outcome is therefore not used as a grouping factor at either the participant or trial level. Instead, trial-level neural responses to the vicariously reinforced threat cue (CSR) and vicarious safety cue (CSS) are used to identify and characterize the neural information distinguishing threat from safety during extinction. A second central objective is to determine how the neural organization of vicarious threat and safety learning differs between SAD and HC participants. SAD may involve alterations in the representation and updating of threat and safety information. The analysis therefore does not assume that a single neural signature generalizes across diagnostic groups. Instead, neural representations are first identified separately within SAD and HC participants, allowing the spatial distribution and discriminability of threat- and safety-related information to differ between groups. The resulting neural profiles are then compared directly to test whether SAD is associated with altered representational geometry, classification certainty, or temporal learning dynamics. The experimental design also includes intranasal oxytocin administered immediately before the extinction phase. Because oxytocin was hypothesized to modulate neural processes involved in threat and safety updating, its administration could alter the very neural representations that the primary analyses seek to identify. Therefore, the initial identification and characterization of threat-safety representations are performed in the placebo condition only, providing an estimate of extinction-related neural representations without potential pharmacological modulation. Participants receiving oxytocin are subsequently incorporated into dedicated analyses testing whether oxytocin alters these neural profiles and whether such effects differ between SAD and HC participants. Within this framework, the primary decoding analysis focuses on the vicariously reinforced threat cue (CSR) and the vicarious safety cue (CSS) because both underwent vicarious learning but acquired different meanings. CSR versus CSS decoding therefore directly tests whether multivoxel neural patterns during extinction distinguish vicariously learned threat from vicariously learned safety. The nonreinforced safety cue (CS−) has a different learning history and is therefore not included as a third class in the primary decoder. Instead, CS− is used as a safety reference condition in subsequent representational analyses, allowing the relative positions of CSR and CSS to be interpreted with respect to an established safety representation and enabling examination of whether CSS becomes more similar to CS− during extinction. L2-regularized logistic regression will be employed to test whether vicarious safety and threat learning are represented by group-specific neural signatures in patients with social anxiety disorder (SAD) and healthy controls (HC) respectively. Next, the neural representations of vicarious learning will be characterized by examining representational geometry, decision-certainty metrics, and single-trial learning dynamics. Then, associations will be tested between these neural profiles and skin conductance responses (SCR), clinical symptoms, and oxytocin modulation. Finally, the neural representations detected during fear extinction will be examined during the reinstatement phase to test whether neural representations of vicarious threat and safety learning are maintained in reinstatement.

candidates.title: The Concept of Identification: An Evaluation of Its Current Status and Significance for Group Psychotherapy
candidates.abstract: [This chapter attempts to present a conceptualization of the process of identification as it occurs during the course of group psychotherapy. The positions of psychoanalytic theory, learning theory, social learning theory, and the psychology of cognition with regard to identification are explored and integrated into a unified conceptual framework.

candidates.title: Co-regulation of learning in simulation: A qualitative exploration of experiences, manifestations, enablers and barriers in medical student simulations
candidates.venue: Focus on Health Professional Education A Multi-Professional Journal
candidates.abstract: Background: Medical education literature offers limited insights into the presence and potential of co-regulated learning (CoRL), where learners interact reciprocally, particularly in collaborative settings such as simulation-based education (SBE). Our qualitative study explores CoRL within SBE in an undergraduate medical program, describing its manifestations, enablers and barriers. Methods: Employing a constructivist approach and reflexive thematic analysis, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 30 participants across four groups: medical students (n = 13), facilitators (n = 5), simulated patients (n = 6) and embedded simulation faculty (n = 6). Results: From this, we built six interconnected themes: (1) simulation design: considered to optimise CoRL, (2) psychological safety: supports CoRL, (3) student agency and vicarious learning, (4) variable between simulation phases (pre-brief, task, debrief), (5) roles and role modelling: impact on CoRL and (6) learning conversations for CoRL. CoRL was described as most prevalent during task performance, indicating substantial learning occurs within the simulation itself, not just during the debrief. Educators can leverage this through SBE by using approaches such as “pause and discuss”. Learner agency was identified as a critical pre-requisite to CoRL, valued by both students and educators. Educators sought opportunities for students to exhibit their abilities, thereby fostering agency and creating openings for CoRL. Discussion: While generally beneficial, CoRL can sometimes manifest in unhelpful ways. This necessitates educator intervention (through role modelling or direct correction) and requires carefully balancing supporting students while still promoting self-regulated learning. We offer practical suggestions for health profession educators seeking to harness the benefits of CoRL in SBE to enhance collaborative learning and prepare future health professionals to be lifelong learners.

candidates.title: Behavioral Biases and Investment Decision-Making Patterns: Evidence of Young Investors from Chitwan District
candidates.abstract: This study is based on the theoretical framework of behavioral finance, prospect theory, and social learning theory. It evaluates the combined effect of financial literacy, investor education, and information on investment decisions among young investors from Chitwan district. The descriptive and causal research design has been used. The data has been collected from 384 investors and analyzed using descriptive, correlation and regression analyses. The study has identified social influence, decision-related factors, and financial literacy as the most significant determinants for investment decisions among young investors. Moreover, it reveals that young investors use a combination of personal knowledge, peer group influence, and access to information to make investment decisions. This study has provided substantial theoretical support for the behavioral finance theory and social learning theory. Finally, this study has provided substantial practical implications for developing rational and sustainable investment behaviors among young investors in emerging markets.

candidates.title: Building a community of practice in a transnational university: The collaborative journey of cross-campus librarians
candidates.venue: Proceedings of the Lancaster University Education Conference
candidates.abstract: For years, cross-border universities continue to provide access to education worldwide through collaborative partnerships especially at the organisational level. The purpose of the paper is to explore how a five (5) year partnership between two librarians from Lancaster University Ghana and Lancaster University have developed to brough together other partners which has shaped academic success especially library services provision to Lancaster University Ghana from the ground level. Relevant literature review topics includes academic literacies as social practice, communities of practice in higher education, etc and adopts Wenger’s (1999) Communities of Practice and social learning systems model as a theory to support the study. The study adopted an exploratory case study approach providing evidence of the collaborative journey between the two librarians, the activities, working structure, support systems and other members of the community of practice within the last five years. The lessons learnt revealed that sustained community of practice enhances social learning, enables timely professional support and access to information, bridges cultural barriers and fosters a sense of shared learning and experiences. It also provides valuable insights for building sustainable collaborations across culturally diverse and dispersed learning environments.

candidates.title: Behavior is Not Enough: A Mechanism-Based Evaluation of Social Norm Emergence in LLM Societies
candidates.abstract: Social norms cannot be identified from behavior alone: the same cooperative equilibrium may reflect shared expectations, strategic incentives, or simple imitation. Yet in multi-agent large language model systems, prior work largely treats behavioral convergence as evidence of norm emergence. In this work, we introduce an evaluation framework that measures agents' reported empirical and normative expectations in addition to behavioral convergence. Through controlled ablations, we test the effect of expectation elicitation and isolate two collective mechanisms central to theories of norm formation---social learning through interaction and social selection through network-based group formation. We further test the stability of these resulting dynamics under adversarial disruption across four LLM families. We find that eliciting expectations increases cooperative contributions, while social learning stabilizes behavior, and social selection reliably identifies cooperators but provides limited behavioral reinforcement. Following disruption, normative expectations and behavioral coordination recover differently. Together, these results show that similar cooperative outcomes can arise from different underlying social processes. By making expectations observable, our framework allows us to attribute each mechanism's contribution separately, offering designers of multi-agent systems a principled basis for selecting the social processes that sustain cooperation.

candidates.title: Drivers of advisory chatbot adoption in smallholder agriculture: A MICMAC analysis of farmer intermediary perceptions in the Sundarbans, India
candidates.abstract: In low-literacy, climate-vulnerable agricultural settings, smallholder farmers rarely evaluate new technologies independently; adoption is mediated through trusted institutional intermediaries. However, the systemic factors driving intermediary-perceived adoption of AI advisory tools remain unmapped. This study applies the Matrice d'Impacts Croisés-Multiplication Appliquée à un Classement (MICMAC) method to examine the systemic drivers of the adoption of generative AI-based agricultural chatbot s , namely, Krishi Dishari, based on the responses of thirty Gram Unnayan Karmi (GUK) intermediaries in the Sundarbans, India, a region facing salinity intrusion and extreme climate challenges. Using a structured bilingual influence matrix survey, the study mapped and classified twelve socio-technical variables by their driving and dependence power. The results indicate that institutional trust is a critical systemic linkage variable, with smartphone access serving as the primary technical driver and social learning emerging as the dominant diffusion mechanism. Furthermore, native language comfort (Bengali) emerged as a key transmission driver, confirming that linguistic accessibility is a prerequisite rather than an enhancement for technology adoption in low digital-literacy contexts. Consequently, this study offers a framework, although transferability warrants exhaustive validation, indicating that AI-based advisory services in vulnerable agricultural settings depend on institutional trust and social learning, not only on technological innovation.

candidates.title: Successful Social Learners Can Choose the Better of Two Options: An Agent-Based Simulation
candidates.abstract: It has been argued that the presence of social learning does not increase population-level fitness because its advantage is frequency-dependent: Social learners cannot flourish unless a sufficient number of individual learners make valid information available. However, recent studies suggest that social learners can achieve higher fitness than individual learners even when individual learners are rare. This study investigated the effects of two mechanisms that confer an advantage on social learners over individual learners: information filtering by social learners and information aggregation through a preference for popular options. Using Smolla et al.’s (2015) model of social learning, which incorporated these two mechanisms, we systematically removed either or both of these mechanisms, rendering the study comparable to a 2 (information filtering: absent vs. present) × 2 (information aggregation: absent vs. present) factorial design. In addition, we tested these effects under the conditions with and without resource competition among agents, which was the original variable of interest in Smolla et al.’s study. The results showed that information filtering conferred a fitness advantage on social learners over individual learners especially when no resource competition was involved. In contrast, information aggregation alone was insufficient to help social learners outcompete individual learners.

candidates.title: Thou Mayest: The Limits of Human Agency
candidates.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
candidates.abstract: This independent literature review examines the limits of human agency through psychological research on genetics, environmental influences, personality development, and intentional personality change. Drawing on research in behavioural genetics, observational learning, gene-environment interaction, personality stability and change, and volitional personality change, the paper explores how inherited tendencies and lived experiences shape individuals while considering the extent to which people can intentionally influence who they become. The review argues that human identity is neither entirely predetermined nor entirely self-created. Instead, psychological evidence suggests that individuals retain a meaningful capacity for intentional change while operating within biological, developmental, and environmental constraints. The philosophical concept of “thou mayest” from John Steinbeck’s East of Eden provides the conceptual framing for this discussion. This work is presented as independent research and is not intended to represent the views or research of any affiliated institution.

candidates.title: Understanding workplace peer support among healthcare assistants providing palliative and end-of-life care at home: a realist review
candidates.abstract: Background: Healthcare assistants delivering home-based palliative and end-of-life care face complex emotional and clinical demands with limited workplace support. Peer support had been suggested as a potential solution, yet no reviews of such interventions exist. Aim: To understand and explain how, why, for whom and in what contexts workplace peer support interventions for healthcare assistants work (or do not work) in palliative and end-of-life care delivery at home. Design: Realist review registered with PROSPERO (registration number CRD42024606133). Data sources: CINAHL, MEDLINE, AMED, Scopus and grey literature with no date restrictions. Searches undertaken November-December 2024. All study designs containing data relevant to programme theory were included. Evidence was assessed for relevance, trustworthiness and rigour. Results: Synthesis of 24 sources from six countries generated 12 context-intervention-mechanism-outcome configurations used to develop initial programme theory. Four workforce outcomes of intervention include: enhanced wellbeing and resilience, reduced loneliness and isolation, development of a sense of community of practice and strengthened role identity. Three intervention strategies: peer-facilitated group meetings, 24/7 peer support access, and informal peer mentorship, create psychologically safe spaces, where individuals feel validated, valued, connected with others, enabling social learning. The intervention elements align with the fulfilment of three basic psychological needs: competence, autonomy, and relatedness. Conclusions: The initial programme theory reveals peer support may address core workforce challenges through psychologically safe peer connections and social learning, aligning with fulfilment of basic psychological needs. It provides a foundation for designing and testing evidence-informed peer support interventions for this workforce.

candidates.title: Celebrity Worship, Social Media, and Substance Use Among Nigerian Students
candidates.abstract: This chapter is based on a systematic literature review that examines how social media engagement influences celebrity worship and substance use among Nigerian university students. Guided by Uses and Gratifications Theory, Social Comparison Theory, and Social Learning Theory, the review analyzed thirty-nine articles selected through PRISMA screening from PubMed and Google Scholar. Findings show that entertainment, identity formation, and social interaction motives increase exposure to algorithm-driven celebrity content, fostering parasocial relationships and celebrity worship. Celebrity-related content also normalizes substance use, particularly alcohol, tobacco, and cannabis. Peer influence, demographic variables, and psychological traits moderate these behaviors. The study recommends strengthening digital literacy, counselling, and public health interventions.

candidates.title: How does cultural transmission impact learning performance? Evidence from the moderated mediation model
candidates.abstract: This study examines how cultural transmission affects learning performance using a moderated mediation model. Cultural transmission shapes individuals’ cognitive and social learning processes, influencing knowledge-sharing behaviours and cultural intelligence. As digital environments increasingly facilitate cross-cultural interactions, digital communication competence is a crucial moderator. Findings from the Education Faculty and the Tourism Faculty indicate that cultural transmission positively affects learning performance, mediated by both knowledge sharing and cultural intelligence. Additionally, digital communication competence strengthens these relationships, enhancing the effectiveness of cultural transmission in digital learning contexts. By integrating these key factors, the study advances understanding of the role of cultural learning in contemporary education. The results provide valuable insights for educators and policymakers to foster inclusive, culturally responsive and digitally competent learning environments.

candidates.title: Integrating Learning Theories for Dynamic Learning Environments
candidates.abstract: This chapter examines major learning theories that have influenced contemporary education, including Behaviourism, Cognitivism, Constructivism, Humanism, Social Learning Theory, Experiential Learning Theory, and Transformative Learning Theory. The chapter argues that no single theory can adequately address the complexity of modern educational environments and proposes an integrated perspective for understanding learning. It analyzes the assumptions, strengths, limitations, and educational implications of each theory and explores their contributions to learner engagement, critical thinking, collaboration, personal development, and lifelong learning. The chapter also examines the relationship between learning theories and assessment practices, educational equity, and the growing role of artificial intelligence in teaching and learning. Through comparative analysis and practical applications, the chapter presents an integrated framework for designing dynamic, inclusive, and transformative learning environments that support both academic achievement and holistic learner development.

candidates.title: Generating Implementation Research Knowledge for Scaling Lifestyle Modification Intervention to Control Hypertension and Diabetes: Lessons from the CoCo-HD Study in Kerala
candidates.abstract: This article describes how a structured lifestyle modification intervention for hypertension and diabetes was scaled within Kerala’s health system, focusing on how implementation knowledge was generated and embedded in routine practice. Grounded in an implementation research approach, the work documents how evidence-informed strategies were continuously adapted through stakeholder engagement, peer-led delivery, and supportive institutional processes. Drawing on qualitative data from stakeholder consultations, document review, and field observations in Janakeeya Arogya Kendrams (basic unit of primary health care centres in Kerala), the article shows how local context, social learning, and power dynamics shaped iterative learning cycles. The findings outline key facilitators and barriers to knowledge use in practice. It offers practical insights for strengthening sustainable non-communicable disease prevention and control programmes in similar settings.

candidates.title: Early VLE Activity and Final Course Results: OULAD Data Documentation
candidates.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
candidates.abstract: This deposit contains an English README, an eight-variable derivative CSV, a data dictionary, a reproducible Python transformation script, processing checks, attribution, and a PDF submission copy. The derivative is based entirely on the real, anonymised Open University Learning Analytics Dataset (OULAD), originally created by Jakub Kuzilek, Martin Hlosta, and Zdenek Zdrahal and downloaded from the UCI Machine Learning Repository (source dataset DOI: 10.24432/C5KK69). The derivative joins studentInfo.csv and studentRegistration.csv on module, presentation, and student identifiers, then aggregates studentVle.csv interactions during course days 0-27 inclusive. It contains 32,593 enrollment records, 28,785 distinct anonymised student IDs, and 22 module presentations. Source '?' markers for unavailable registration dates are represented by blank cells; zero early clicks are valid derived counts, not missing values. DDI-Codebook 2.6 concepts guide the human-readable documentation; the project is not a validated DDI XML record. The package supports descriptive, observational learning-analytics work and does not report a causal result. It is distributed under CC BY 4.0 with attribution to the original OULAD creators and a clear description of the transformations. The editable project is at https://github.com/Liliwovo/oulad-real-data-readme.

candidates.title: How Is Farmer Cooperation Possible? Interaction, Identity, and Community Capacity in a Chinese Rural Community
candidates.abstract: ABSTRACT How can cooperation emerge in communities where institutional enforcement is weak and social relations are fragmented? Drawing on a longitudinal case study of Village L in rural China (2017–2021), this paper develops a five‐stage process model that explains the endogenous emergence of cooperation. Moving beyond incentive‐ and institution‐centered accounts, the analysis shows how cooperation is dynamically generated through a sequence of interactional mechanisms: initiated by exemplary action, expanded through observational learning and symbolic reinforcement, deepened through deliberative coordination that activates a collective identity, and stabilized through ritualization into a cooperative cultural structure. The study demonstrates that farmers' agency is not a pregiven individual capacity but an emergent, relational outcome of interactional processes unfolding over time. By examining how interaction, identity formation, and cultural stabilization are linked in practice, this article treats cooperation as an emergent social accomplishment rather than a fixed equilibrium or a problem of institutional design. It develops a process‐based explanation of how community capacity and collective agency are gradually built in rural settings marked by weak institutions and fragmented social relations. In doing so, the study speaks to ongoing debates in rural sociology about how cooperation is generated and sustained in everyday social life.

candidates.title: How negative parenting relates to adolescents’ perceptions of older adults: the roles of empathy and intergenerational contact
candidates.abstract: Introduction Grounded in social learning theory, this study examines how negative parenting practices are associated with adolescents’ perceptions of older adults and investigates the roles of empathy and intergenerational contact in this process. Methods Data were collected from 2,011 Chinese adolescents using a three-wave longitudinal design. Structural equation modeling was used to test the hypothesized relationships. Results Negative parenting was significantly associated with less favorable evaluations of older adults on both the warmth and competence dimensions. Empathy mediated these relationships. Intergenerational contact further moderated the association between empathy and adolescents’ perceptions of older adults. Specifically, the indirect effects of negative parenting through empathy varied according to adolescents’ levels of intergenerational contact. Discussion These findings highlight family socialization as an important developmental context for adolescents’ perceptions of older adults and identify empathy as a key socio-emotional mechanism linking parenting experiences to intergenerational cognition.

candidates.title: Media's Role in Shaping Gender Norms and Perceptions: A Conceptual Review
candidates.venue: Budapest International Research and Critics Institute  (BIRCI-Journal): Humanities and Social Sciences
candidates.abstract: This study examines the role of media in shaping gender norms and perceptions, with particular attention to how media representations construct, reinforce, negotiate, and potentially transform understandings of masculinity and femininity. The study adopts a qualitative secondary-data approach, drawing on existing scholarly literature, empirical studies, theoretical perspectives, and documented evidence on gender representation across social media, with particular consideration of the Nigerian media context. The study argues that media should not be understood as a passive reflection of existing social realities but as an active cultural institution that participates in the construction and circulation of gender meanings. The reviewed evidence indicates that women continue to be disproportionately represented through appearance, domesticity, caregiving, emotionality, and subordinate roles, while men are frequently associated with authority, economic success, independence, dominance, and emotional restraint. Such recurring representations can normalise restrictive gender expectations through processes of observational learning and cumulative media exposure. In the Nigerian context, existing evidence suggests that gendered patterns identified in international scholarship are also evident in Nollywood and other media forms, although audiences interpret these representations through culturally specific frameworks. The study concludes that media remains a significant force in shaping gender perceptions, but its influence can also be mobilised for social transformation. Achieving more equitable gender perceptions therefore requires media representations that move beyond visibility towards diverse, meaningful, and non-stereotypical portrayals of women and men.

candidates.title: Cognitive and non-cognitive developmental outcomes in age-homogeneous and age-heterogeneous preschool classrooms: a systematic review
candidates.venue: European Early Childhood Education Research Journal
candidates.abstract: Age composition in pre-primary education, that is, the degree of age homogeneity or heterogeneity within classrooms, is one structural factor that may influence children's developmental outcomes. This systematic review, conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines, synthesises evidence from 23 empirical studies selected from 629 screened records. Studies were organised into two analytical domains: (1) cognitive outcomes and (2) noncognitive outcomes, the latter including natural school- or childcare-based studies and supplementary dyadic or controlled peer-interaction studies. Findings on cognitive outcomes are inconclusive. Some studies indicate modest advantages of age-homogeneous classrooms in selected domains, particularly preliteracy, early numeracy, executive functions and school readiness, but these effects are inconsistent and appear to depend on study design, outcome measures, instructional context and operationalisation of age composition. Findings on noncognitive outcomes more consistently suggest potential benefits of age-heterogeneous settings, particularly for peer interaction, social participation, cooperation, helping, role differentiation and observational learning. However, these findings require cautious interpretation because of methodological heterogeneity and the inclusion of dyadic or small-scale studies. Overall, age heterogeneity should be understood not as an independent causal factor, but as a structural condition that may create opportunities for peer-mediated learning and social interaction under specific pedagogical and organisational conditions.

candidates.title: I nfluencing F actors in A ttracting and R etaining A udiences for H onor of K ings L ive S treaming on D ouyin
candidates.venue: Advances in Economics Management and Political Sciences
candidates.abstract: With the development of short-video platforms and game live streaming, Douyin has gradually become an important arena for game content dissemination, audience interaction, and the formation of platform stickiness. As a popular MOBA mobile game, Honor of Kings combines competitive suspense, entertainment value, learning value, and social value in its live-streaming content. Using a narrative literature review approach, this paper examines the question of how Honor of Kings game live streaming on Douyin attracts audiences and increases their continuance watching intention. It reviews existing studies related to Honor of Kings players' motivations, mechanisms of game live streaming, Douyin platform mechanisms, streamer performance, and community operation. The review finds that previous literature has separately revealed the importance of game content value, electronic word-of-mouth, observational learning, uses and gratifications, algorithmic recommendation, gamification mechanisms, technological affordances, user identification, live-streaming humour, and streamer labour. However, these dimensions have rarely been integrated into the specific context of Honor of Kings live streaming on Douyin. This paper argues that audience attraction and retention in Honor of Kings live streaming should be comprehensively understood from three aspects: game content, streamer interaction, and platform mechanisms. Future research can further explore how these factors influence audience engagement and continuance watching intention jointly.

candidates.title: Application of Sociocognitive Psychology Counseling Techniques Alberd Bandura Faces Student Academic Failure
candidates.venue: Jurnal Ilmu Pendidikan dan Sains Islam Interdisipliner
candidates.abstract: Students often face academic failures during their studies, academic failures in college, such as graduation delays, trial failures, unplanned leave, and dropouts This can trigger psychological impacts such as stress, anxiety, low self-esteem, and loss of motivation to learn. This article aims to: (1) analyze the psychological dynamics of students who experience academic failure; (2) examine key concepts in sociocognitive psychology theory, especially self-efficacy, modeling, and self-regulation; and (3) explain the application of sociocognitive counseling techniques in helping students bounce back from failure. This study uses a narrative literature review of research on student academic failure, and its application to sociocognitive theory. The literature was searched through Google Scholar, PubMed, and PsycINFO, and then analyzed thematically to integrate relevant concepts into the explanatory framework. The results of the study showed that academically failing individuals were prone to psychological disorders, but were able to recover by strengthening self-efficacy, observational learning, and self-regulation strategies. Sociocognitive theory provides a powerful conceptual framework for understanding and facilitating adaptive behavior change. The application of sociocognitive-based counseling techniques such as modeling, mastery experiences, goal setting, and cognitive restructuring has been shown to be effective in improving self-confidence and learning strategies. These findings provide important implications for educational counselors and college institutions in designing counseling services oriented towards recovery and psychological capacity development.

candidates.title: It is time to revisit the external determinants of state terror
candidates.abstract: Authoritarian regimes are frequently influenced by external policies and transnational relationships when shaping domestic repression strategies. Existing empirical research has largely focused on demonstration and diffusion effects, emphasizing how governments emulate repressive practices observed abroad. Similarly, recent scholarship on authoritarian cooperation and regional organizations has argued that interstate cooperation strengthens authoritarian rule and facilitates repression through exchanges of information, expertise, resources, and strategic support. We distinguished theoretically between observational diffusion and cooperative interaction and examine empirically how each shapes state terror. Using spatial autoregressive combined models and global data on authoritarian regimes from 1947 to 2010, we found that demonstration via observational diffusion among institutionally similar regimes is generally associated with higher levels of state terror, whereas contemporaneous interdependence among such regimes is associated with lower levels. These results are broadly consistent across different specifications of the dependent variable. Our findings suggest a more nuanced relationship between interstate cooperation and repression: Cooperation may enhance authoritarian control while reducing reliance on the most extreme forms of violence. More broadly, the results indicate that diffusion-centered approaches may conflate observational learning with broader forms of authoritarian interdependence, thereby mischaracterizing the consequences of external influence for state terror.

candidates.title: Our Shared History
candidates.abstract: This chapter describes the development of ideas from the 1980s to the close of the twentieth century that balanced cognitive perspectives with social approaches and led to more nuanced proposals for the role of grammar instruction in L2 development. Given research in the 1980s showing that learners who had never experienced explicit L2 instruction often showed developmental plateaus at intermediate proficiency levels, together with increased interest in the communicative functions of form-meaning relationships, there emerged calls for L2 grammar instruction as a “focus on form” to be achieved incidentally within communicative, task-based lessons. Meanwhile, an increased application of social learning theories to L2 development in the 1990s led to proposals for a more holistic view of explicit grammatical knowledge, communicative language use, relevant content, and social relationships as important factors in L2 development. Together, these movements suggested by the turn of the millennium a need for a multi-faceted understanding of language and language learning to explain how cognitive and social systems interact with each other.

candidates.title: Modeling Daily Digital Experiences in Adolescents: A Multilevel Latent Class Analysis of Social Media Engagement Patterns and Exposure to Alcohol-Related Content
candidates.abstract: This study used multilevel Latent Class Analysis (mLCA), a day-level, person-centered approach to examine adolescents’ social media engagement, and associated it with exposure to alcohol-related content. Participants were 302 adolescents (Mage = 16.21) who completed 21 days of ecological momentary assessment and weekly surveys. Using multilevel latent class analysis, we identified six distinct engagement types: No Use, Passive Use, Liked/Reacted, Moderate Engagement, Discussion, and High Engagement. Sixty-two percent of adolescents spent most days in one dominant class. Exposure to alcohol-related content from peers or followed accounts predicted more active engagement days, consistent with social learning processes. Exposure from peers was related to temporary social media disengagement, whereas exposure from followed accounts predicted reactive use. Reliance on self-report and the absence of private-messaging measures are noted limitations. Findings highlight dynamic daily processes linking online engagement with substance-use risk contexts.

candidates.title: TRADISI PANGELEMIJIAN DI PURA BEDUGUL DESA PUJUNGAN KECAMATAN PUPUAN (Kajian Pendidikan Agama Hindu)
candidates.abstract: Although Balinese Hindu religious traditions serve as non-formal educational media, ritualpractices are increasingly performed as formal customary obligations without deepphilosophical understanding. Furthermore, while previous studies on Pangelemijian mostlyfocus on pitra yajna (death rituals), research examining Pangelemijian as a uniqueagricultural ritual remains unexplored. Addressing this gap, this study aims to describe theimplementation and philosophical meaning of the Pangelemijian Tradition at Pura Bedugul, identify its Hindu Religious Education values (Tattwa, Susila, Acara), and analyze its socio-educational implications. Using a qualitative method with observation, structured interviews, documentation, and literature study, data were analyzed through Historical-Cultural,Ceremony System, Value, and Social Learning theories. The findings reveal that thistradition, performed during Purnama Sasih Kapat with a unique deer-head mask dance("klincang-klincung"), symbolizes gratitude to Dewi Sri and agricultural protection. Itembeds core Tattwa, Susila, and Acara values, functioning as a non-formal learning mediumthrough social observation, reinforcing local cultural identity, and strengthening communitysocial solidarity.

candidates.title: Developing Gender Effective Coaches: Addressing the Knowledge to Application Gap
candidates.abstract: In recent years, there has been an increase in opportunities for women and girls in sport in Canada. Yet, biases, stereotypes, and norms about gender remain deeply embedded within sport culture (Goorevich & LaVoi, 2025), affecting girls and women across the landscape. The purpose of this doctoral dissertation was to provide coaches with evidence-based tools for their pursuit of gaining confidence in addressing and deconstructing gender beliefs that affect their coaching practice through three interconnected studies. The studies included: (1) the narrative exploration of gender beliefs and the impact they have on coaching methodologies, athlete interactions, and self-confidence; (2) the creation of a gender-related coaching self-efficacy scale; and (3) the exploration of coaches' knowledge-to-action processes through the lens of social learning. In this pursuit, I aimed to support coaches in their development of gender responsive and transformative practices to better address the needs of girls in sport. A pragmatic philosophical orientation, informed epistemologically by social constructionism, was used in this dissertation research. In line with pragmatism, a mixed methods design approach was executed taking into consideration four theoretical frameworks including a combined model of coach self-efficacy (Feltz et al., 1999) and coach effectiveness (Horn, 2002; 2008; Côté & Gilbert, 2009), Wenger's (1998) theory of social learning and communities of practice, and Goorevich and LaVoi's (2025) continuum of gendered sport coach discourses. The results of this inquiry are presented through three articles. In the first study, entirely qualitative in nature, I present composite vignettes that explored the diverse and context-dependent experiences of coaches coaching girls, further nuanced by the lived realities of women coaches. Data collection consisted of focus groups with 20 coaches ranging in sport and coaching experience. This narrative inquiry aims to illustrate how coaching philosophies and practices are socially shaped through gendered discourses operating within sport. As a result of the findings from this examination, potential items for the scale development study were created. The need for more opportunities for coaches to develop self-awareness regarding their gender biases, reflect, and deconstruct their gender beliefs to make changes to their coaching practices was also highlighted as future areas for growth in coach education. The second study was conducted through a mixed methods approach, consisting of the development and primary validation of the Girls-Centred Coaching Self-Efficacy Scale (GCSES). The scale development process followed previously established methodological guidelines (i.e., Boateng et al., 2018) with an initial 87 items being created through theory-driven item construction, coach focus groups (n = 20), expert review (n = 6), and cognitive interviews with coaches (n = 4). The revised instrument after this process included 31 items and was administered to 216 sport coaches. An exploratory factor analysis supported a four-factor structure for 23 final items accounting for 54.9% of the variance with strong internal consistency across subscales (⍺ = .80-.92). Subscales include: (1) gender literacy in coaching, (2) understanding gendered sport experiences, (3) fostering gender-inclusive sport, and (4) girl-centred coaching practices. The findings from this study provide evidence for the GCSES to be used as a context-specific tool for evaluations and interventions aimed at advancing gender responsive and transformative coaching practices. The third study used a mixed methods quasi-experimental design, exploring coaches' knowledge-to-action processes related to their girl-centred coaching self-efficacy through a combined online and social learning intervention. Twenty-five coaches took part in one of two conditions over a five-month period, either completing the series of Coaching HER's foundational eLearning modules by themselves or engaging in a community of practice (CoP; Wenger, 1998) concurrent with the eLearning modules. Coaches in both groups took the GCSES pre- and post-intervention, and data were analyzed using mixed ANOVAs. Participants in the CoP condition were also invited to partake in a focus group (n = 6) grounded in the value creation framework (VCF; Wenger-Trayner & Wenger-Trayner, 2020) to explore how value was created through their participation in the CoP. Effect and contribution data were collected throughout the intervention period (Wenger-Trayner et al., 2019). Although the study was underpowered to detect statistically significant differences between conditions, coaches who engaged in the CoP condition demonstrated small trends of mean improvements across all GCSES factors compared to the eLearning condition. Qualitative data, presented through two value creation stories (VCSs; Wenger-Trayner et al., 2019) and individual value cycle examples, aided in providing insight into the GCSES results as well as how coaches in the CoP condition translated learnings into changes to their practices. Altogether, the findings from the final study in this dissertation suggested that engagement in a CoP fostered opportunities for self-reflection, accountability, and contextual application of knowledge. Recommendations included the continued use of social learning in tandem with eLearning for coaching education to better support coaches' knowledge-to-action processes and the value of mixed methods research in this domain. The results of this doctoral dissertation aim to provide an evidence-based foundation for understanding, measuring, and supporting coaches' development toward more girl-centred and gender-equitable coaching practices. Collectively, the findings advance both theory and practice by offering practical tools, empirical evidence, and a conceptual framework to guide future coach education, research, and organizational efforts aimed at fostering meaningful and sustainable gender equity in sport.

candidates.title: Loss-domain preferences and protective climate adaptation: evidence from grape farmers under increasing precipitation
candidates.abstract: Understanding how farmers make adaptation decisions under increasing rainfall-related risks is critical for effective climate risk management, yet evidence remains limited on the role of behavioural factors in shaping these decisions. Using data from a field experiment and a survey conducted in major grape-producing regions in China, this study investigates how risk preferences across different domains affect farmers’ willingness to adopt adaptation measures in response to anticipated increases in rainfall and rainy days. We find that farmers differ in both risk attitudes and outcome sensitivity across the gain and loss domains, but only preferences in the loss domain significantly affect adaptation intentions and increase the likelihood of adopting rain covers as a protective measure. The effect is heterogeneous across age, farm size and exposure to social learning. These findings suggest that climate adaptation measures may be more effectively promoted when framed as tools for reducing potential losses rather than enhancing expected returns. They also highlight the role of demonstration and peer-based learning in easing concerns over potential losses and improving the uptake of adaptation practices among smallholders.

candidates.title: Adolescents in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Navigating the Risks of Overuse
candidates.venue: Journal of Communication Sustainability and Empowerment
candidates.abstract: Adolescence is a sensitive developmental period marked by heightened neurobiological plasticity, identity formation, and socio-emotional learning. As generative artificial intelligence becomes embedded in adolescents’ daily lives, existing frameworks for digital harm, built around screen time and social media exposure, may not capture its distinct psychological affordances. This study aims to reframe adolescent AI overuse as a qualitatively distinct developmental and relational exposure, rather than an extension of screen time. Using a narrative synthesis of developmental science, relationship science, and documented public cases published between 2018 and 2025, the study examines how AI reliance intersects with five developmental domains: emotional regulation, social learning, identity formation, autonomy, and attachment. The synthesis identifies recurring conceptual risks externalized coping, recalibrated relational expectations, externally validated identity, deferred autonomy, and displaced attachment while noting that direct empirical evidence in adolescent samples remains sparse. The study proposes a working definition of adolescent AI overuse and an interim clinical, educational, and policy framework, offering a conceptual foundation for the empirical research this area still lacks.
